Give each function its own file
rather than bundling multiple functions into one file.
This applies to exported functions, internal helpers,
and test helpers alike ---
the only exception is a trivial two-line wrapper
that is inseparable from its caller.

### R packages

Under `R/`, name the file after the function it contains:
`simulate_data()` lives in `R/simulate_data.R`.
A private helper that is more than a two-liner
still gets its own file, named after the helper,
even if only one caller uses it.

### Why

A file with one function is easier to find,
easier to diff
(a change to one function does not sit inside
an unrelated grep hit for a different one),
and matches how `git blame` and code-review tools
attribute changes.
Bundling unrelated functions into one file ---
because they were added in the same PR,
or because an existing file happened to be open ---
accumulates unrelated concerns over time.

### Adding to an existing multi-function file

When adding a function to a file that already holds others
(common in older code that predates this convention),
put the **new** function in its own file
so at least new code follows the convention going forward.
Splitting every pre-existing function out
is a separate, larger refactor.

### Relationship to function decomposition

When decomposing a large function
(@sec-function-decomposition),
place each extracted helper in its own file
rather than above or below the caller in the same file.
The caller file then contains only the orchestration function,
and each helper is independently findable and testable.
